description:
Looking for a motivated, multidisciplinary team passionate about space exploration, technology, and innovation.
Interested in collaborating, sharing ideas, and developing creative solutions to real-world challenges using NASA data.
summary: Lost & Found: Solar System Branch is a browser game for school-age space fans. The player is the new clerk at the Lost & Found office of the Solar System, where the shelves hold 18 machines NASA sent to the Moon, to Mars and into deep space. Each machine has a case file: why it was sent, how it worked, what it found and where it is now. Six flagship files let the player run the machine: fire a laser at the Apollo mirrors and time the real echo, or drive Spirit backwards on its broken wheel until it digs up silica-rich soil. The other twelve let the player fly the mission: drag its real events onto a path and the machine travels to its final resting place. This answers the challenge by teaching through how the hardware actually worked instead of through lists of facts. It matters because these "abandoned" machines made discoveries that today's missions build on, and kids rarely hear their stories.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The home screen is an office at night, with a round window to space and three shelves: The Moon, Mars and Deep Space. Clicking a machine opens its case file with four short tabs (Why it was sent, How it worked, What it found, Where it is now) and a handwritten note from the office archivist. The six flagship files also show a real NASA photo. Archie, a desk robot, offers a guided tour.

Six flagship files have a hands-on mini game:

- Laser reflector: aim at one of the three Apollo mirrors, fire a pulse and wait for the echo. The delay (about 2.3 to 2.8 s) comes from the Moon's real distance at that moment.

- Apollo descent stage: at launch time, drag each item to where it belongs: it stays on the Moon or it flies home.

- Surveyor 3: click the parts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean removed in 1969 (about 10 kg) on a drawing of the lander.

- Spirit: the right front wheel has failed, so you drive backwards, dragging it, uncover bright soil and analyse it (about 90% silica, a sign of past water).

- Ingenuity: hold a button to spin the rotors up in thin Martian air and let go at the right moment. Below about 2,400 rpm it won't lift, and above 2,700 it's unsafe.

- Voyager 1: see its live distance and light travel time, then send a greeting that travels across the screen (clearly marked as a simulation). On 18 November 2026 it reaches one light-day from Earth, and the game counts down to that moment.

Twelve more files (the Lunar Roving Vehicles, Sojourner, Opportunity, Viking 1 and 2, Phoenix, InSight, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 and 11, and Kepler) are mission journeys: the player drags the mission's real events onto a path, stop by stop, and the machine's drawing travels along it to where it rests today, on Mars, on the Moon or drifting in deep space. Seven "Fact or Myth?" dispatches test famous claims, such as the "My battery is low and it's getting dark" quote, which Opportunity never sent, or whether Voyager 1 has really left the solar system. A reserved shelf asks the player what their generation will send into space. That entry, and the player's progress (a Solved stamp on every finished file), stays only in the player's own browser, and a Clear my progress button starts the game over.

HOW IT WORKS

It is a static web page (HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript) with no server, no install and no login. All text lives in one content file (content.json), and every stamped fact carries a source that can be checked on the Sources page. A Python validator blocks publishing if any fact, number or game value lacks a source. It also checks that our NASA JPL Horizons table matches NASA's published one light-day moment (they agree within 4 minutes). Distances come from Horizons tables saved for November 2026 to March 2027, so the page never guesses. An automated test plays every file in headless Chrome and takes screenshots on desktop and mobile.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

Kids learn by doing the engineering, not by memorizing it. Story and fact stay clearly apart: handwritten notes are our story and carry no numbers, while stamped facts are real and checkable under "Sources". Because the content sits in one file, new machines and languages can be added without touching code.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python, headless Chrome for testing, Google Fonts (Literata, Fira Sans, Cousine, Playpen Sans; open font licenses), and spacecraft drawings made for this project with SI assistance.
